assets.topic: The Death List on the Dry-Cleaner's Pad
assets.visual_frame_description: You are in a sweltering Louisiana living room two days after the murders. Homicide photographs lie on a table, and beside them is the actual small promotion pad from a local dry-cleaner. The top page is covered with names: some crossed out, some underlined, some circled, connected by intersecting lines, grouped in columns of three or four. A forensic analyst points a pen at the scribbled word 'sky' written next to several names.
assets.player_mission: Scrub every notation on the pad and decode what the killer was doing. Determine what the page documents and why one name in particular, a Malibu resident, demands immediate protective action.
key_concepts: Perry's pad was a written plan narrowing candidates to ten people he intended to kill.
Name after name was crossed out, re-written, circled, underlined, or linked by lines as Perry weighed who lived and who died.
Perry wrote the word 'sky' near the names of people he had already killed.
The list included names in Louisiana, one in Texas, one in Washington, D.C., and one in Malibu.
When Perry finished the list, only the Malibu name, de Becker's client, remained.
Written plans of this kind function as documented pre-incident indicators of intent and selectivity.
At four P.M. on July 20, 1983, investigators found five bodies in Jennings County, Louisiana, and the lead suspect was Michael Perry.
Perry had told a psychiatrist that the client was 'evil and should be killed.'
A few words Perry had written on that sheet changed everything and triggered an unprecedented evacuation of the client's home.
Perry's parents were among the homicide victims, and a high-powered rifle and at least two handguns were missing from their home.
assets.theory_summary: This scrub tests pre-incident indicators in written form: the list is a record of escalating, selective intent that precedes the predicted outcome. De Becker presented the pad as the artifact that converted a theoretical hazard into a concrete, actionable one, showing that documentation of a plan is itself behavior worth reading.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Documents and written notations left behind by the subject
assets.question: What does the pad most clearly reveal about Michael Perry's intent toward the Malibu name on the list?
assets.correct_cue: The pad is a working death list: roughly ten final targets selected from a larger field, with killed victims marked by the word 'sky', and all competing names eliminated until only the Malibu client remained. Read together, the circling, crossing, underlining, and line-connections show deliberate selection and ranking rather than random scribbling, and completion of the list with the client's name still on it signals that she was the culminating target. This is the evidence that led de Becker to evacuate her within the hour, an action he never took before or since.
distractors: The pad was Perry's shopping list of survival supplies for living in the wilderness.
The pad recorded phone numbers of people Perry planned to call for help after the murders.
The word 'sky' was a code word for a meeting place in the Louisiana bayou.
assets.underlying_psychology: People who intend violence sometimes externalize the plan on paper, converting fantasy into ranked, reviewed, and rehearsed targets. The documenting behavior is a pre-incident indicator: the killer's own writing shows narrowing, prioritizing, and record-keeping of lethal intent, which both predicts action and reveals whom the danger has concentrated upon.

assets.visual_frame_description: Helicopter rotors thump over the chaparral ridges of the Malibu hills. Tracker Tom Brown, a wiry quiet man with the seriousness of Clint Eastwood, crouches beside a game trail while armed PSD agents wait. He points at a bent weed, an unsettled pebble, and faint shadows in the dust, then asks the agents to bring out the plaster cast of a shoeprint taken at the Louisiana murder scene.
assets.player_mission: Study the channel of environmental disturbance around the client's property. Identify which subtle signals Brown reads and what his art demonstrates about intuition built from small details.
key_concepts: Tom Brown had authored more than a dozen books on tracking and had been called in to search for dangerous men before.
Brown asked specific questions about Perry: what food he liked, whether he ate meat, whether he smoked, what his shoes and clothes were like, and what his hair was like.
From a helicopter he over-flew an area where firemen had reported a makeshift camp and pointed out spots for PSD agents to check on foot or horseback.
Brown could tell where a person had walked, slept, even paused.
His intuition was informed by a subtle series of signals: bent weeds, unsettled pebbles, shadows in the dust, and other details most people would look right past.
Brown explained: 'When somebody moves something in your house, you notice it. When somebody moves something in the woods, I notice it.'
A PSD agent carried a plaster cast of a shoeprint from the murder scene and Brown would compare it to small ridges or depressions in the dust.
While on the ground, Brown was accompanied by armed PSD agents and taught them some of what he knew about tracking.
Perry had checked tracking books out of the Jennings County Library, including one by Tom Brown called The Search.
assets.theory_summary: This scrub tests intuition as pattern recognition over a channel most observers disregard: micro-disturbances in terrain. De Becker portrayed Brown's 'marvel' as perception of environmental anomalies that register as signals once the perceiver knows what to look for, evidence that seemingly odd details can locate and identify dangerous people.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Environmental disturbance: terrain, vegetation, and dust altered by human passage
assets.question: What made Tom Brown able to track Michael Perry in terrain where everyone else saw nothing?
assets.correct_cue: Brown read deviation: a bent weed where none should bend, an unsettled pebble, and shadows in the dust reveal where a person walked, slept, or paused. He did not guess; he compared micro-signatures, even asking for the plaster casting of Perry's shoeprint to match against ridges and depressions in the dust. Because Perry himself had read Brown's books, the tracker's expertise was the one technique that could penetrate the survivalist's evasion, and it led agents to a shelter overlooking the road the client drove every day.
distractors: Brown relied on a GPS-linked drone system that scanned the hills from above.
Brown detected Perry by the scent of a cooking fire and followed the smoke at night.
Brown interviewed local residents to triangulate Perry's daily movement patterns.
assets.underlying_psychology: Intuition here is not magic but informed noticing: the mind reads small anomalies against an implicit baseline of how things normally look. De Becker used Brown to show that what seems like a mysterious gut sense is often rapid comparison of subtle signals that the untrained eye literally overlooks.

assets.topic: The Gate Intercom Slip in the Phone Interview
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim Washington jail office. De Becker, unprepared, holds a phone to his ear; through the line, Michael Perry speaks in a fast, street-wise patter. On a scroll of subtitles, Perry first insists he has never been to the client's house, then, moments later, volunteers an exact description of the gated entrance: a little drive-in theater intercom, a push button, a red light, a camera out front.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the verbal channel of the interview. Compare Perry's denials against the details he offers unprompted, and decide which statement the observable evidence actually supports.
key_concepts: Perry lied without hesitation, sounding like a fast-talking, street-wise con man.
He denied ever having been to the client's house: 'I don't think I've ever been to her house, sir. I don't think so. I really don't.'
When asked about California, Perry said he just went swimming at the beach and did some camping.
It is common for criminals to avoid giving information someone wants, often precisely because it is wanted.
Perry then gave up the lie and described the entrance to the client's home exactly, including the gate intercom, the red light of the security program, and the camera out front.
His denial and his accurate description cannot both be true.
Perry said the house might have had an underground shelter and that it was a big place.
He claimed he rang the bell, said 'This can't be the place,' and felt a 'strong, strong feeling' of respect for the ancient place.
This unguarded slip occurred in a conversation de Becker entered without preparation.
assets.theory_summary: This scrub tests the contradiction between a subject's denial and his volunteered sensory detail: specific, unprompted interior knowledge of the very place he claims never to have visited marks the denial as false. De Becker noted that criminals withhold information precisely because it is wanted, making the unguarded accurate description the truer signal of what Perry had actually done.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Verbal channel: the consistency between claims and volunteered descriptive detail
assets.question: Which moment in the call most reliably reveals that Perry really had been to the client's property?
assets.correct_cue: The gate intercom description. Having flatly denied visiting the house, Perry spontaneously reconstructed the approach as a 'little drive-in theater deal' with a push-button intercom, a red light, a camera out front, and a feeling that the place was ancient and would have an underground shelter. A person who had never stood at that gate could not produce such scene-specific, functionally correct details, and the ease of the description contrasted sharply with the stilted earlier denials.
distractors: Perry's question about whether the house had an underground shelter proved he was fantasizing about the property.
Perry's admission that he rang the bell and left before anyone answered proved the denial truthful.
Perry's claim that the red light was 'part of the security program' showed he had read about the house in a magazine.
assets.underlying_psychology: Deception strains at the point of unprompted sensory recall: rehearsed lies stay vague while lived experience produces concrete operational detail. The mechanism is the tension between the effortful construction of a false account and the automatic retrieval of actually encoded memories, which leaks through when the liar relaxes his guard.

assets.visual_frame_description: Sun block letters on the screen split the frame. Top: a Malibu resident tells a deputy that a strange man knocked at his door asking questions about 'the magic movie star' and then headed up the hill on foot. Bottom: a phone booth outside a Beverly Hills shop, beside it a small newspaper item reporting that the client frequented that shop, and a phone record showing a collect call Perry made to his parents from that very booth.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the pattern of Perry's discrete behaviors around the client's world. Identify the through-line that connects inquiring about the star, the hut's vantage point, and the phone records, and rate what it says about Perry's capability.
key_concepts: A Malibu resident reported a strange man knocking on doors and asking questions about 'the magic movie star.'
Perry had spent time in a makeshift camp in the hills that firemen had spotted some months before.
Agents found a shelter of gathered wood and twigs containing the sleeve of one of the client's record albums, a fork, matches, and a bola made of two rocks tied to a rope.
From the shelter, Perry could see the clearing where the client drove by each day on her way to and from home.
Phone records revealed Perry had called his parents collect from the Malibu library during visits to California.
Six months earlier a small newspaper had reported the client's frequenting a particular Beverly Hills shop, and Perry had called his parents from the phone booth right outside that shop.
De Becker concluded they were dealing with a capable stalker.
Efforts in Malibu included daily interviews of people who might have seen Perry and asking local shopkeepers to report anyone inquiring about the client.
Brown's aerial overflight covered areas where the firemen had seen the makeshift camp, and PSD agents checked the spots on foot or horseback.
assets.theory_summary: This scrub tests stalking as cumulative information-gathering: discrete behaviors such as asking questions, living under surveillance vantage points, and calling home from locations the target frequents connect into a single pattern of capability and planning. De Becker used these converging details to argue that the obsessive pursuit was deliberate, patient, and geographically literate.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Pattern of the subject's location-based behaviors and information-seeking
assets.question: What single conclusion do the resident's report, the hill shelter, and the phone records support?
assets.correct_cue: That Perry was actively surveilling the client in Malibu, not merely drifting. He gathered information in person (door-knocking and asking about 'the magic movie star'), positioned himself where he could watch her daily routes (the shelter overlooking the clearing), and used print media plus public telephony to track her movements (the newspaper item and the collect calls from the library and the phone booth outside the shop). Together these behaviors show a systematic, patient surveillance operation, which is why de Becker rated Perry a capable stalker and kept the Malibu search at full strength even while pursuing other leads.
distractors: The behaviors show Perry was only trying to phone the client directly.
The incident shows Perry was a drifter who happened to camp near several locations by chance.
The evidence demonstrates that Perry had abandoned his pursuit of the Malibu target.
assets.underlying_psychology: Stalking is often a project of information and proximity: the pursuer's intelligence-gathering, positioning, and repetition of behaviors reveal the strength and direction of the fixation better than any single encounter. Observing where the subject puts himself, and where he seeks data, exposes the target concentration that precedes the act.

assets.visual_frame_description: A cheap hotel room, the Annex, a mile and a half from the U.S. Supreme Court. Nine television sets are crammed into the space, all plugged in, all tuned to static. On one set the words 'My Body' are scrawled in red marker; on several screens giant eyes have been drawn; along the side of one set the client's name is written boldly. Detective Kilcullen and de Becker stand in the doorway, silent.
assets.player_mission: Scrub the channel of the subject's living space and possessions. Decode what the clutter of televisions, eyes, and the client's name reveal about Perry's state of mind and the direction of his obsession.
key_concepts: Perry took a cheap room at the Annex Hotel, about a mile and a half from the Supreme Court.
Room 136 was a 'bizarre museum of the media age,' a work of pop-art connecting violence, madness, and television.
Nine television sets were crammed into the tiny room, all plugged in, all tuned to static.
On one set Perry had scrawled the words 'My Body' in red marker.
Several sets had giant eyes drawn on the screens.
One television had the client's name written boldly along its side.
Perry told Risler that the only sense he could make of television was by watching channels with nothing on.
Perry's father had told him, 'When I go to work, I leave my eyes at home,' and Perry had legally changed his name from Crab to Eye.
Perry told de Becker he had seen the client's eyes change color in an HBO special and feared she might be a witch.
assets.theory_summary: This scrub tests the diagnostic reading of a subject's private space: symbolic arrangements of objects externalize the delusion and the fixation. De Becker read Room 136 as a self-portrait in which static, eyes, and the client's name converge on Perry's lifelong terror of being watched and his transference of that imagery onto the star he stalked.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: The subject's possessions, living arrangements, and symbolic arrangements of his environment
assets.question: What do the televisions, the drawn eyes, and the client's name on the set most plausibly reveal about Michael Perry?
assets.correct_cue: That the client had been absorbed into the center of Perry's private delusional world. The nine static-tuned televisions, on one of which he wrote 'My Body' in red and on which he drew giant eyes, replay his belief that he could 'read' the blank channels, while the eyes echo the father who 'left his eyes at home' to spy on him; writing the client's name on a set grafts her onto that world. The room shows a man whose fixation was not entertainment but the maintenance of a private cosmology with the stalked star at its heart, matching his fear that she was a witch whose eyes changed color.
distractors: The televisions show Perry was preparing to broadcast his confession to the nation.
The eyes on the screens prove Perry was an accomplished artist using his time in hiding productively.
The static-tuned sets demonstrate that Perry wanted to watch the news of his own manhunt.
assets.underlying_psychology: Living spaces become behavioral evidence: how a subject arranges objects, and which symbols he repeats, externalizes cognitive content that he will not articulate. Here the obsessive's environment performs his delusion, converting television, eyes, and a name into a shrine that tracks the logic of the fixation from private imagery to targeted violence.

assets.topic: Audit of the GdeB-Perry Phone Call
assets.visual_frame_description: A case-file interface opens on your screen: a transcript of the July 31 telephone call between de Becker and the just-captured Michael Perry, with a time-synced behavioral log running beside it. Timestamps tick past as the fast-talking voice denies, deflects, then suddenly surrenders the lie and describes a Malibu gate intercom in precise detail.
assets.player_mission: Run the deception audit on Perry's account. Compare his baseline, his denials, and his volunteered detail, then render the correct verdict about whether he had been to the client's house and what his silence told you.
key_concepts: Within an hour of the arrest, Detective Kilcullen called de Becker and offered to let him talk to Perry.
De Becker entered the interview without preparation.
Perry lied without hesitation, sounding like a fast-talking, street-wise con man.
Perry denied visiting the house, denied being in California beyond beach swimming and camping, then described the gate intercom, red light, and camera exactly.
It is common for criminals to avoid giving information someone wants, often precisely because it is wanted.
Perry described the client's movie face and said she looked like his mother in 1961, the day of the heater incident.
Perry drifted off into silence and de Becker waited quietly for him to speak again.
Perry feared the client might be a witch and might 'do some damage' to him for speaking.
The siren call of a guest stealing a radio had led to the warrant check that identified Perry.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the interplay of denial, volunteered detail, and silence in a single deceptive account: Perry's rehearsed denials crumbled under the weight of accurate sensory recall, while his silences carried the emotional truth of the obsession. De Becker's method was patience and listening, letting the subject's own words and pauses convict him.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Had Michael Perry really been to the client's Malibu home, and what did the silence after his denials reveal?
assets.subject_baseline: Perry, when interviewed, was a fast-talking, street-wise con man who lied without hesitation; a survivalist who hated to be looked at and had eluded a nationwide search for eleven days.
observed_nonverbal_log: 00:00 - Denies ever being at the house: 'I don't think I've ever been to her house, sir. I don't think so. I really don't.'
00:40 - Denies real California purpose: 'Well, I just went swimming at the beach, you know, and did some camping; that's all.'
01:30 - Volunteers unsolicited explanation: the client's movie face looked like his mother's face in 1961 when she walked into the room; 'It ruined the whole thing, you know.'
02:10 - Changes subject, denies again, then gives up the lie and describes the gate intercom, red light, camera, and the impression of an underground shelter.
03:20 - Becomes quiet, drifts off into silence; de Becker waits quietly.
04:00 - Speaks of the obsession: 'nothing, nothing had ever stuck to my mind like that. And even, you know, even today, even today, even today...'
04:40 - Reveals fear: the client's eyes changed color on HBO; she might be a witch and might 'do some damage' to him for saying so.
06:00 - Ends the call: 'I'm under arrest right now, I just want you to know that... some sort of big accident, some theft or something like that, which I didn't do.'
interrogation_transcript: Perry: I don't think I've ever been to her house, sir. I don't think so. I really don't.
GdeB: Really?
Perry: Right. I really don't.
GdeB: Have you ever been to California at all?
Perry: Well, I just went swimming at the beach, you know, and did some camping; that's all.

Perry: You know they had like a little drive-in theater deal [the gate intercom], you know, you push the button. And a red light [part of the security program]. And I had the impression that the house might have had an underground shelter, and it's a big place. And I rang the bell, and there was a camera out in front and everything.
Perry: And even, you know, even today, even today, even today...
Perry: On her special, on HBO, I saw her eyes change color. Her eyes change color a lot. ... That girl might be a witch, you know. She may do some damage to me if she hears me saying this.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Deception detected on the visit to the house; the accurate gate-intercom description confirms Perry had been to the property, and his silences and asides reveal genuine obsessive fixation rather than mere evasion.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The blanket denials ('I really don't think so') match the baseline of a fast-talking man accustomed to lying, so their wording alone proves little. The decisive evidence is the unprompted operational detail: a gate intercom described as a 'little drive-in theater deal,' a red light, a camera, a big house that might have an underground shelter. Only someone who had stood at that gate could assemble that scene from memory, and the richness of the detail directly contradicts the earlier denial. The follow-on silence and the repetitious 'even today, even today, even today' show the interview had touched the obsessive core, confirming that the falsehood protected the very fixation the conversation exposed.
distractors: Perry was telling the truth because he never admitted to being at the house.
Perry was attempting to manipulate de Becker into lenient treatment for the pending charges.
Perry's silence indicated he was withholding information about other intended victims on the list.

assets.topic: Audit of the Risler Jail Interview
assets.visual_frame_description: A Louisiana jail conference room. Sociologist Walt Risler sits opposite Michael Perry, who is agitated and sweating. The screen shows a running log: Perry refuses topics, says his head is 'filled with vomit,' demands 'Tell her to stay away from Greece,' asks his attorney to leave, takes Risler's hands, and claims an atomic missile hidden in the swamps will explode if he is executed. You must grade the performance.
assets.player_mission: Audit whether Perry's bizarre statements are strategic deception or genuine psychosis. Weight his behavior, his private-session request, and his concluding claim, then deliver the verdict de Becker's team reached.
key_concepts: De Becker arranged for Walt Risler, a full-time consultant to the office for more than a decade, to interview Perry in jail.
Perry was an accomplished survivalist who had read books on the subject from the Jennings County Library.
Perry's fears as a child grew into an elaborate delusion that dead bodies were rising from a chamber beneath the floor of his house.
Perry told Risler: 'Tell her to stay away from Greece. That's all I want to say to you now, man. I'm feeling sick, so sick; my head is just filled with vomit.'
Perry said he could only make sense of television by watching channels with nothing on.
Perry asked his attorney to leave so he could speak with Risler in private.

Perry took Risler's hands and explained that if he was executed it would trigger the explosion of an atomic missile hidden in the swamps near town: 'So you see, getting me out of here is important to everyone. I'm just trying to save lives.'
Perry ended the interview standing: 'Oh, man, my head is filled with vomit. You can just see how fucked up my head is, can't you, from the things I think?'
De Becker concluded: 'Perry was not faking insanity — this was the real thing.'
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the distinction between malingered and genuine psychotic content: Perry's delusions were internally consistent, privately confessed, and loaded with idiosyncratic personal symbols rather than shaped for an audience. De Becker and Risler concluded the psychosis was authentic, grounded in a documented lifetime of delusional thinking rather than a courtroom performance.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Was Perry's extraordinary testimony an attempt to manipulate the interviewers, or genuine psychosis?
assets.subject_baseline: A mentally ill man with a documented history: childhood delusions of the dead rising under his house, a legal name change from Crab to Eye, years of stalking, and a recently committed homicide spree ending with five murders.
observed_nonverbal_log: 00:00 - Enters agitated, refuses to discuss the future of de Becker's client beyond a cryptic warning.
00:20 - Says: 'Tell her to stay away from Greece. That's all I want to say to you now, man. I'm feeling sick, so sick; my head is just filled with vomit.'
00:50 - Shifts to a favorite topic, television: 'After a while it got so that the only sense I could make of television was by watching channels with nothing on.'
01:20 - Asks his attorney to leave the room so he can speak privately with Risler.
01:40 - Takes Risler's hands and warns that if he does not get out of jail 'there will be hell to pay,' and that execution would detonate an atomic missile hidden in the swamps near town.
02:10 - Declares he is 'just trying to save lives' by asking to be freed.
02:30 - Stands to end the interview, citing the vomit filling his head and the twisted things he thinks.
interrogation_transcript: Perry: Tell her to stay away from Greece. That's all I want to say to you now, man. I'm feeling sick, so sick; my head is just filled with vomit.
Risler: (asks about television)

Perry: Man, TV is really fucked up lately. I don't know what it means. After a while it got so that the only sense I could make of television was by watching channels with nothing on. I could read them and make more sense than what was happening on the programs.

Perry: (attorney dismissed; taking Risler's hands) If I don't get out of jail, there will be hell to pay. If I was executed, it would trigger the explosion of an atomic missile hidden in the swamps near town. So you see, getting me out of here is important to everyone. I'm just trying to save lives.
Perry: Oh, man, my head is filled with vomit. You can just see how fucked up my head is, can't you, from the things I think?
assets.correct_diagnosis: Genuine psychosis, not manipulation: the threat to de Becker's client, the missile fantasy, and the self-flagellating conclusion were expressions of a real delusional system.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: A rehearsed manipulator crafts content for the audience's benefit; Perry instead sought privacy (asking his attorney to leave) before volunteering material that implicated himself, and his imagery was consistent with his documented delusions across decades, from the dead rising beneath his childhood home to watching static channels 'read' the world. The missile story served no discernible legal advantage and ended with self-disgust rather than a demand. Risler and the team weighed this evidence and concluded Perry's insanity was real, shaping both the trial strategy and the later Supreme Court medication dispute.
distractors: Perry fabricated the missile story to frighten the prosecution into a plea deal.
Perry was rehearsing testimony he planned to use at his trial to win an insanity defense.
Perry was testing Risler's gullibility to see how much bizarre behavior the consultants would tolerate.

assets.topic: Audit of Warren P. in the Malibu Hills

He is lifted onto the dirt, looking directly at de Becker, who recognizes him: not Michael Perry, but Warren P., the lovesick pursuer from years past. As officers walk him to a sheriff's car, he repeats, 'I had no idea the security would be this tight.'
assets.player_mission: Audit Warren P. as a subject of the response. Classify his risk, his role in the incident, and the lesson his capture teaches about the pursuit of the primary suspect.
key_concepts: Warren P. was another mentally ill pursuer whom the firm had interviewed years before and heard from occasionally.
He was a lovesick man who hoped to marry the client.
De Becker recognized him immediately; he was not Michael Perry.
Warren was 'worthy of assessment' but without sinister intent; more a tragic figure than a dangerous one.
His bad luck had carried him through years of effort and across thousands of miles to the client's home, the mecca of his romantic delusions.
He arrived on the worst possible afternoon for a visit, during the full-scale Perry manhunt.
He repeated: 'I had no idea the security would be this tight.'
The client already had a team of PSD agents assigned for about a year, partly because of the predicted arrival of Perry and partly because of another murderous stalker, Ralph Nau.
A tabloid-style reading of a 'crazed fan' would miss that Warren posed no planned violence.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests risk discrimination between pursuing individuals: arrival at a target's home does not by itself equal lethal intent. De Becker's assessment separated Warren P.'s benign romantic pursuit from the lethal threat of Perry, showing that hazard classification must weigh intent, history, and capability rather than the mere fact of proximity.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: What is the correct classification of Warren P. when he is caught on the client's hillside?

assets.correct_diagnosis: Warren P. was a non-lethal pursuer caught in the wrong place at the wrong time: worthy of assessment, without sinister intent, and utterly unaware of the manhunt he had wandered into.

The audit therefore classifies him as a low-hazard pursuer, while flagging that his very presence proves how many obsessed people orbit a public figure and why any single arrest on the property should not be assumed to be the primary subject.

assets.topic: Audit of the King of the Hills
assets.visual_frame_description: Moonlit brush in Malibu. A team of PSD agents follows a suspicious trail through a gully, flashlights held parallel to the ground to reveal patterns in the dust. They come upon a shelter of gathered wood and twigs, empty, containing a record-album sleeve, a fork, matches, and a bola. Then movement: a man with a mess of dark hair approaches, wearing a crown of twigs and leaves. Pounced on from all sides, he yells, 'I'm the king, I'm the King!'
assets.player_mission: Audit the crowned man and the shelter. Determine who this pursuer was, what his shelter revealed, and how his capture relates to the hunt for Michael Perry.
key_concepts: Three PSD agents searching with Tom Brown's techniques found a suspicious-looking trail near the client's property.
Agents shone their flashlights parallel to the ground to show patterns in the dust.
The team moved silently through a gully into dark brush, hoping to find Perry and on some level hoping not to.

The shelter was built of gathered wood and twigs and contained filthy clothes, the sleeve of one of the client's record albums, a fork, matches, and a crude bola made of two rocks tied to the end of a rope.
Through a clearing the shelter looked directly onto the road the client drove each day to and from home.
The approaching man had a mess of dark hair, more than could have grown in the time Perry was at large.
He wore a crown made of twigs and leaves and yelled 'I'm the king, I'm the King!' as he was handcuffed.
He was another mentally ill pursuer who was there to watch over the client, his 'queen.'
He was not Michael Perry.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests reading a subject's contrived role identity as evidence of delusion: the twig crown and the kingly declaration are not camouflage but the outward sign of an erotomanic fantasy. De Becker showed that such pursuers insert themselves into elaborate imagined relationships, and that their contrivances, however theatrical, are real delusional content, not cunning deception.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: What did the twig crown, the 'I'm the king' declaration, and the shelter reveal about this pursuer?
assets.subject_baseline: Unknown to the team before the encounter; a man living rough in the hills who had built a shelter close to the client's daily driving route and collected items connected to her.
observed_nonverbal_log: 23:40 - Agents follow a suspicious trail through a gully into dark brush, flashlights parallel to the ground.
23:55 - They reach a shelter of gathered wood and twigs; nobody is inside.
00:00 - Inside the shelter: filthy clothes, the sleeve of one of the client's record albums, a fork, matches, and a bola of two rocks tied to a rope.
00:05 - From the shelter opening, the team sees the clearing where the client drives by each day.
00:10 - Sounds of someone moving through the brush; the team holds its breath in the moonlight.
00:15 - A man with a mess of dark hair approaches, wearing a crown of twigs and leaves.
00:16 - Pounced on from all sides, he yells, 'I'm the king, I'm the King!' as he is handcuffed.
interrogation_transcript: Man: I'm the king, I'm the King!
Agent: (restraining him) Who are you watching here?
Man: (indicating the client) My queen. I'm here to watch over my queen.
GdeB: (later assessment) Still another mentally ill pursuer, living in my client's orbit during the Perry case.
assets.correct_diagnosis: A mentally ill pursuer with an erotomanic delusion of royalty over the client, living in a vantage-point shelter for her; a genuine hazard to assess but emphatically not Michael Perry.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The declaration of kingship, delivered under physical restraint, is not a strategy for evading arrest but the eruption of a fixed fantasy role: he cast himself as king and the client as his queen, over whom he 'watched.' The shelter discredits chance: positioned to observe her daily route, stocked with a relic of her (the album sleeve) and the tools of rough living, it shows intentional proximity and occupation of a surveillance position. The hair length alone — too long to have grown since Perry fled — and the man's own words closed the identification: this was a separate pursuer whose delusion placed him beside her, and whose capture while Perry remained at large underscored how many obsessed men surrounded the property.
distractors: The crown was a clever disguise to slow down the pursuing agents.
The man was Michael Perry wearing new hair and a costume to evade recognition.
He was Warren P. returning to the property after his earlier arrest.

assets.topic: Audit of the Watermelon in the Oldsmobile
assets.visual_frame_description: A dusty green Oldsmobile sits in a D.C. tow yard beside a warehouse. Detective Kilcullen and de Becker walk up as an officer peers through the window into the front seat and recoils: 'It's covered in blood.' The door opens and a dark, pulpy liquid clings to the fabric upholstery. Then someone notices the watermelon seeds scattered on the floorboards.
assets.player_mission: Audit the apparent blood evidence in the car and determine what actually stained the seat. Weigh the first glance against the physical clues and issue the correct finding.
key_concepts: Perry had driven Chester Perry's green Oldsmobile, dusty from its long drive, all the way to Washington, D.C.
An officer looked in at the front seat and recoiled, saying, 'It's covered in blood.'
There was a dark, pulpy liquid sticking to the fabric upholstery.
Opened, the car revealed watermelon seeds on the floor.
It was not blood on the seat; it was watermelon juice.
Rather than pause to eat somewhere, Perry had bought a watermelon and eaten it with his right hand as he sped along the highway toward D.C.
Perry had driven those same highways eastward while the nationwide manhunt was in full swing.
Car in hand, Perry had traveled a mile and a half from the Supreme Court to the Annex Hotel, where Room 136 awaited.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests perceptual verification against physical evidence: the first visible impression ('blood') was corrected by material clues (seeds, pulp consistency) that identified watermelon juice. De Becker's account shows how even trained observers jump to alarming conclusions, and how a single overlooked detail can reverse a dramatic misreading of a scene.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: What was the dark, pulpy liquid staining the front seat of the Oldsmobile?
assets.subject_baseline: Perry, a survivalist on the run, driving a borrowed family car across the country without stopping for meals; a man of extreme efficiency who avoided pausing anywhere recognizable.
observed_nonverbal_log: 10:00 - Kilcullen and de Becker arrive at the tow yard holding Perry's car.
10:02 - An officer looks through the window into the front seat and pulls back: 'It's covered in blood.'
10:03 - Dark, pulpy liquid is visible sticking to the fabric upholstery.
10:04 - The door is opened for a closer look.
10:05 - Watermelon seeds are seen on the floor.
10:06 - Assessment corrects: the stain is watermelon juice, consumed with the right hand while driving.
interrogation_transcript: Officer: It's covered in blood.
Kilcullen: (opening the door) Look at the seeds. Watermelon.
GdeB: (assessing) He bought a watermelon and ate it with his right hand as he sped along the highway toward D.C. He never paused to eat somewhere.
Officer: (relieved) That's juice, not blood.
assets.correct_diagnosis: The staining was watermelon juice, not blood; Perry ate a watermelon with his right hand while driving and never stopped.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The recoil ('It's covered in blood') is exactly what the first glance suggests: a dark, pulpy, reddish liquid on fabric is the visual signature of blood. But the physical evidence overrides the impression: watermelon seeds on the floor establish the source, the consistent pulp texture matches watermelon rather than dried blood, and Perry's documented pattern of non-stop movement explains why he would eat in the car, one-handed, at highway speed. The finding demotes a would-be crime-scene shock to a mundane detail, while still confirming the same portrait of the suspect: a man who would not stop for anything short of his destination.
distractors: The stain was blood Perry failed to clean from the murders before driving cross-country.
The stain was vomit from Perry's claimed illness during the drive.
The stain was oil leaked from the Oldsmobile's engine onto the seat.

assets.topic: Where in America Is Michael Perry?
assets.visual_frame_description: A war room in the TAM office at night. Maps of Louisiana, Washington D.C., and the Malibu hills are pinned to the walls. De Becker stands before the team; the death-list pad is blown up on a screen, and a file fanned out shows the collect calls, the hill shelter, and the Pope's-eye notes from Walt Risler, who is headed toward the conclusion that D.C. and Malibu are a Perry-esque Sodom and Gomorrah. The bass of a sheriff's helicopter thuds somewhere off-screen.
assets.player_mission: Run the prediction battle: allocate the manhunt's attention across three hypotheses about Perry's location, commit to the strongest prediction, and manage the decision when the arrest finally comes through a trivial call.
key_concepts: Perry was assumed to be in one of three places or somewhere between them: Louisiana, Washington, D.C., or Malibu.
Predicting that Perry might act out violently was simple; the hard questions were how he would encounter his victims and how patient he would be.
Walt Risler, a pioneering thinker in predicting violence and a full-time consultant for more than a decade, studied the murder scene and Perry's writings.
Risler found in the living-room crib a shrine: a crucifix, a pillow, three family photos face down, a wall plaque of the Virgin Mary, and a ceramic crab.
Risler concluded that Washington, D.C. and Malibu were a Perry-esque Sodom and Gomorrah and predicted Perry was on his way to the capital to kill Justice O'Connor.
On that basis de Becker contacted Tom Kilcullen, a seasoned D.C. homicide investigator, and filled him in on the case and Risler's opinion.
The Malibu search continued daily with interviews; the nationwide hunt spanned California, Nevada, Texas, D.C., New York, and even Africa.
On July 31, police in D.C. responded to a hotel dispute call; a routine warrant check identified the patient man standing before the officer as Michael Perry.
Perry's list had included Justice O'Connor because, as he explained, 'no woman should be above a man.'
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests prediction under uncertainty with multiple plausible locations: weighing converging evidence to commit to one hypothesis while keeping parallel protection in place. De Becker showed that the prediction that seemed least glamorous — a capital-city targeting forecast by his consultant — proved exactly right, and that the arrest arrived through a mundane procedure rather than a dramatic confrontation.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is prediction in manhunt management: a violent subject with known fixations can be located by reasoning about his targets and his patience, and a minority prediction defended by evidence can beat the loudest leads.
assets.stage_1_observation: Eleven days into the hunt, evidence crowds the room: the death list with names in Texas, D.C., and Malibu; collect calls from the Malibu library; a hill shelter overlooking the client's route; and Risler's shrine-reading of the crib at the murder scene, where he concluded D.C. and Malibu were a 'Perry-esque Sodom and Gomorrah' and predicted the killer was traveling to kill Justice O'Connor. Meanwhile, USA TODAY headlines blare 'Mass Killer Still at Large' for someone else, and the client waits in a safe house.
assets.stage_1_question: Where did the evidence point, and which prediction did the team commit to despite its distance from the most dramatic leads?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Risler predicted Perry was heading to Washington, D.C., to kill Justice O'Connor — placing her name and the client's in his paired 'Sodom and Gomorrah' — and the team acted on that forecast by briefing D.C. homicide investigator Tom Kilcullen, while maintaining, not abandoning, the Malibu and Louisiana searches.
assets.stage_2_intervention: On July 31 a sleazy D.C. hotel calls police about a guest who stole a radio. An officer interviews two 'derelict oddballs' and concludes nothing illegal happened; the only step left is the routine warrant check. As he waits, a man stands patiently before him. You must now decide whether to treat this minor dispute as the tail of the case or as its climax.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The routine warrant check is exactly the moment to run: the patient man standing in front of the officer is Michael Perry, and the case that consumed eleven days ends with a computer search on his name, not a stakeout or SWAT raid. The win comes from refusing to skip standard procedure in boring circumstances, because hazards routinely surface in unremarkable settings.

assets.topic: Protecting the Client Under Extreme Hazard
assets.visual_frame_description: The screen splits into three timelines. Left: July 20, a Los Angeles hotel lobby, a PSD agent waving de Becker to a car. Center: the client's Malibu home, sheriff's helicopter buzzing, police closing the street while de Becker answers her anxious questions beside the PSD backup car. Right: a few days later, downtown D.C., de Becker at a desk with a phone in his hand, about to talk to the captured Michael Perry.
assets.player_mission: Fight the protection battle: decide when personal action replaces delegation, how to move the client without terrorizing her, and how to handle the sudden moment when the subject himself is on the line.
key_concepts: De Becker maintains a policy of not telling clients about particular cases unless there is something they must personally do.
The precaution of full-time bodyguards at the client's home existed in part because the office predicted Perry might show up, and in part because of another murderous stalker, Ralph Nau.

Based on a few words Perry wrote on the sheet of paper, de Becker did something he'd never done before or since: he called the client to pack for a few days because he'd be there within half an hour to pick her up.
De Becker concluded the team could not adequately protect her at home even with bodyguards, and took her to a hotel via a loading dock and service elevator.
A room near the client's suite was modified into a security command center, and she was later moved to a safe house rented out of state.
In the interview that followed, de Becker entered without preparation and simply let Perry talk.
Perry volunteered the motive ('she looked like my mother back in 1961') and the accurate gate description without being asked.
After conviction, doctors refused to medicate Perry just so he could be lucid for his execution, and the Supreme Court ruled he could not be forced to take the medication.
The case ended not with a gunfight but with a phone call, and de Becker walked into the TAM office to say 'I just got off the phone with Michael Perry.'
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests calibrated communication and protection decision-making under extreme hazard: withholding information until the client must act, then escalating to a decisive personal intervention when the subject's documented planning overwhelms on-site defense. De Becker's case shows timing, transfer of protective posture, and a listening-based interview yielding the fullest account of a killer's motive.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is protective calibration: matching the client's knowledge and movement to the assessed threat, escalating to evacuation only when the subject's plan and capability make fixed-site protection inadequate, and seizing the interview opportunity the instant it opens.
assets.stage_1_observation: Two days into the case, the picture has sharpened: Perry is an accomplished survivalist who has visited Los Angeles several times; his parents were killed and a high-powered rifle and two handguns are missing; he told a psychiatrist the client was 'evil and should be killed'; and the pad found at the murder scene shows his list narrowed until the client's name alone remained among the ten. The client is at her Malibu home, ringed by a full PSD team, unaware of the case details — de Becker's policy is not to tell clients about a case unless there is something they must personally do.
assets.stage_1_question: Why did de Becker — for the only time in his career — call the client to pack for a few days and personally drive her to a hotel, despite an existing team of full-time bodyguards?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because the note on the pad converted a general hazard into a documented, executed plan: the killer had narrowed a working list to ten targets, marked his kills, and left the client's name standing, while proven capability (repeated visits, firearms, survival training) and elapsed travel time meant he could be closing in. A static defense could not beat a determined planner, so the protective posture had to change: the client was moved through a loading dock and service elevator to a hotel with a security command center, and later to an out-of-state safe house, with information given only for what she needed to do.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Weeks of tension later, the manhunt ends with a phone call: Perry is in custody in D.C., and Detective Kilcullen offers de Becker the chance to speak with him right now, unprepared. You must decide how to open the conversation with the man who has dominated every waking thought of the team for eleven days.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Take the call and simply talk: ask direct questions, don't script the interview, and above all wait through his silences. Perry lied about visiting the house, then volunteered the exact gate-intercom description and, unprompted, the 1961 mother-face motive. The listening posture — including de Becker waiting quietly while Perry drifted off — pulled out the most accurate account of a killer's motive in the entire case, and it ended the emergency not with a SWAT team but with a conversation.
